name: Jean Bartik
milestone_by_age_26: Selected in 1945 at age 21 as one of the six original programmers of ENIAC, the world's first general-purpose electronic digital computer, and co-led the team that publicly demonstrated it in February 1946.
early_history_summary: Born Betty Jean Jennings in rural Gentry County, Missouri in 1924, the sixth of seven children of a schoolteacher-farmer father. She graduated from Stanberry High School at age 16 in 1941 and earned a B.S. in mathematics from Northwest Missouri State Teachers College in 1945. Immediately upon graduation she was hired by the University of Pennsylvania as a human computer to calculate ballistic trajectories, and within months was selected as one of six women to program the newly completed ENIAC.
family_context_summary: Born into a large farming family in rural Missouri; her father was both a schoolteacher and a farmer, and many family members were teachers. The family was not wealthy but valued education.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a schoolteacher and farmer; no connection to computing or advanced technology. Family tradition of teaching.
evidence_summary: Jean Bartik came from a rural Missouri farming family with no computing connections but a strong educational tradition. She graduated with a math degree at age 20 in 1945 and was immediately hired by the Moore School at the University of Pennsylvania, which was the epicenter of early electronic computing. Within months she was selected as one of six women to program ENIAC, the world's first general-purpose electronic digital computer. The wartime mobilization created an unusual opportunity for a young woman from rural Missouri to access the frontier of computing. The six-woman team developed fundamental programming techniques through intense collaboration.
starting_point: Born in 1924 in rural Gentry County, Missouri to a large farming family; father was a schoolteacher and farmer, sixth of seven children.
current_position: Died March 23, 2011 at age 86 in Poughkeepsie, New York; final roles included real estate agent after earlier career as a pioneering computer programmer on ENIAC, BINAC, and UNIVAC.

trajectory.event: Graduated from Northwest Missouri State Teachers College with a B.S. in mathematics and was hired as a human computer at the Moore School, University of Pennsylvania.
Selected as one of the six original programmers of ENIAC, the world's first general-purpose electronic digital computer.
Co-led the ENIAC programming team for the public demonstration of the computer in February 1946, which made headlines nationwide.
Led a group of programmers to convert ENIAC into a stored-program computer, a major milestone in computing history.
Joined Eckert-Mauchly Computer Corporation and worked on the BINAC and later UNIVAC, the world's first commercial computer.
Earned a master's degree in English from the University of Pennsylvania.
Inducted as a Fellow of the Computer History Museum and received the IEEE Computer Society Computer Pioneer Award.
Died on March 23, 2011, in Poughkeepsie, New York, from congestive heart failure complications.

The family emigrated to Philadelphia in 1924 where her father worked as a stonemason. She graduated from Chestnut Hill College in 1942 with a mathematics degree, was hired as a human computer at the Moore School, and in 1945 was selected as one of six ENIAC programmers.
